Faculty Senate Executive Committee Bill #2026-2027-01
October 15, 2026 Faculty Senate Meeting - FOR ACTION
(Introduced at the September 17, 2026 Faculty Senate Meeting)
Creates standard process for committee formation
Approved by FSEC 08/31/26 and 10/7/26 (as amended)
Reviewed by CBUM 09/28/26 and 10/8/26 (as amended)
Legislation effective date: Spring semester 2027
Rationale: The limited number of faculty senators, in combination with University-Manual-mandated committee staffing requirements, can make it difficult to staff an expanding number of standing committees. This makes it important to ensure that additional standing committees and subcommittees, whose charges and memberships are proscribed in the University Manual, are created only in response to a significant and sustained need. In contrast, special committees can be created by the Faculty Senate to address pressing issues. While there is no limit to the length of time a special committee can exist, the faculty senate must vote to reauthorize each special committee each year.

This legislation mandates that a newly formed committee must exist as a special committee for at least three (3) years before legislation reconstituting it as a standing committee or subcommittee can be considered by the Faculty Senate. Such legislation must be accompanied by language specifying the charge and membership of the standing committee for inclusion in the University Manual. This change provides time for the Faculty Senate to 1) consider whether a new standing committee or subcommittee is truly warranted; and 2) craft an appropriate and achievable charge for the body.
This legislation does not mandate that a special committee must be reconstituted as a standing committee after three years. It is also not retroactive, i.e., all existing standing committees and subcommittees remain unchanged.
This original version of this legislation was introduced for discussion at the 9/17/26 Faculty Senate meeting. The final version has been revised as follows in response to faculty/staff comments.

1. Remove language mentioning joint committees. Joint committees are, by definition, created in concert with the administration (staffing, wording, charge, power balance). While the faculty and administration may choose to designate a joint committee as a special joint committee subject to the rules and procedures detailed below, the power to do so does not rest exclusively with the faculty senate.
2. Identify the assessment process and who conducts it. Added language to §4.12.1 specifying that the Special Committee’s self-assessment shall be reviewed by FSEC. FSEC which shall use it as the basis for a recommendation to the Faculty Senate to vote on whether the Committee should dissolve, continue as a Special Committee, or be reconstituted as a permanent Standing Committee or Subcommittee.
3. What happens if no reauthorization vote is taken before the end of the AY? Added language to §4.11.1 specifying that all Special Committees are annually authorized by vote of the Faculty Senate. A Special Committee that has not received an affirmative reauthorization vote (assuming that no duly authorized extension has been granted) within one year of authorization shall be dissolved.

4. After the third-year review, can a reauthorized Special Committee apply to change its status? Added language to §4.12.1 specifying that a Special Committee must wait at least two years after its third-year review (i.e., be in its fifth consecutive year of operation) before requesting that the Faculty Senate reconsider reconstituting it as a Standing Committee or Subcommittee.

FSEC Proposal - Introduction Only - Bill #2026-2027-FSEC-02 - Changing deadlines for course withdrawals.
Kristy Snow, CELS Academic Advisor, presented her draft bill which has been favorably reviewed and advanced by FSEC.

It was noted that advisors are attuned to students’ frustration with early withdrawal deadlines because, in many instances, they have yet to glean a robust assessment of whether or not they can be successful in a course.
They are forced to make guesses about how they might perform and many withdraw too soon, in an abundance of caution, which often has grave consequences.
Because withdrawals can impact things like full-time status, housing and financial aid, graduation date, etc. students would benefit from a more complete snapshot of how they are doing before making such decisions.
There were a number of questions from the floor and, while most senators were supportive of the move to extend the "withdraw without extenuating circumstances" period, there was concern that changing the deadline from three to eleven weeks was a bit extreme.
Data was presented from peer institutions who all have later deadlines than URI.
Other concerns centered around possible increased demand for faculty signatures, whether or not deadlines for accelerated and summer/J-term courses will also be adjusted (the current proposal only addresses 3

regular semester-long courses), and what impacts later withdrawals might have on group work of fellow students and on IDEA completions for faculty.
Sen.
Buxton suggested that the bill proposers perhaps also consider expanding the deadlines and relaxing the requirements for taking courses Pass-Fail rather than for a letter grade.
Students could then still keep earning credits so impacts on full-time status, degree completion dates, financial aid, etc. are somewhat mitigated.
Advisor Snow noted the usefulness of the feedback and she hopes to address many of the concerns in the next draft of the bill. d.
FSEC Proposal - Introduction Only - By-Laws Amendment - Bill #2026-2027-FSEC-01: Transitioning Special Committees to Standing Committees.
Senate President Preisser presented the draft bill which will be reviewed by CBUM before the next senate meeting when it will return for a vote.
He explained that, in recent memory, the senate has created new permanent committees without a complete understanding of their long-term need, the durability of their charge and resources available to help them address it, and the most appropriate membership composition to ensure the committee’s enduring success.

The proposal calls for a three-year “trial period,” wherein a special committee is created (through senate action, but without requiring an amendment to the university manual or by-laws) that performs a self-assessment during its third year and makes recommendations to the senate about whether to continue as a special committee, disband, or convert to a permanent committee.
This new process would apply to joint and sub-committees as well as senate standing committees.
Feedback was generally positive and it was noted that once a permanent, standing committee makes its way into the university manual and/or by-laws, it becomes difficult and cumbersome to refine its mission, charge and membership.
The new process would provide time to adopt the best possible manual language for new committees and ensure that practical concerns which can only be understood by seeing a committee in action are addressed from the start. e.

Creation of a College Liaison Special Committee
Effective starting spring 2027
The College Liaison Special Committee shall consist of ten senators, one from each college that elects Faculty Senators and one from the Library, who are referred to as the ‘Liaison’ from their unit to the Faculty Senate. If the Faculty Senate votes to approve creation of this Special Committee in fall 2026, senators from each college/Library will select one of their number to serve during the spring 2027 semester in the role of Liaison. Following senate elections in May 2027, senators from each college/Library will again select one of their number in August to serve during the 2027-2028 academic year in the role of Liaison. Liaisons may be re-elected but must be a current senator. The Senate President and FSEC will ask for volunteers to chair this committee on a one-year basis and identify a chair for vote by the Faculty Senate at its September meeting.

College Liaison Committee members are charged with ensuring that faculty in each college are informed of pertinent university-level matters and communicate senate- and college-level concerns in both directions. Liaisons attend all-college faculty meetings and will be given the opportunity to give a report on senate activities. The Liaison also attends meetings of the Faculty Senate in their role as a current senator.
Liaisons have two responsibilities in addition to attending college- and senate-level meetings. First, Liaisons provide a brief monthly update regarding senate/university-level matters to faculty in their college. Second, Liaisons represent their college on the College Liaison Committee. This committee meets at least once per semester to address issues requiring inter-college coordination. The College Liaison Committee is a Special Committee of the Faculty Senate, chaired by the Vice President of the Faculty Senate who serves as a non-voting member.
